title: Principles of Financial and Managerial Accounting

questions.q: What is the effect of a company's accounting department maintaining high ethical standards?
choices: The company's accounting information will increase in value.
The company can hire fewer accountants to do the same amount of work.
The company's accounting information will decrease in value.
The company can report more favorable results in its financial statements.
questions.explanation: Ethical accounting = trustworthy data = investors/lenders/regulators rely on it = info is MORE valuable. Ethics doesn't reduce workload or manipulate results — those are red flags.

questions.q: Why might employees be interested in their company's financial accounting information?
choices: Financial statement data provide item-by-item product cost information.
Financial statement data provide detailed internal budget information.
Financial statement data are often used in determining employee bonuses.
Financial statement data are used to record long term liabilities.
questions.explanation: Employees care because bonuses and profit-sharing tie directly to financial performance. Product costs and internal budgets are managerial accounting (private), not financial statements.

questions.q: Which group establishes financial accounting rules in the United States?
choices: Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)
International Accounting Standards Board (IASB)
American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)
Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
questions.explanation: FASB = US GAAP rules. IASB = international (IFRS). AICPA = profession organization, doesn't set rules. IRS = tax rules only.

questions.q: Which report is one of the three primary financial statements?
choices: Statement of the accounting cycle
Statement of stakeholder funds
Statement of cash flows
Statement of management accounting
questions.explanation: The Big 3: Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Statement of Cash Flows. (Statement of Retained Earnings is sometimes counted as a 4th.)

questions.q: A company paid $5,000 cash in advertising costs. How does this transaction affect the paying company's accounting equation?
choices: Assets increase by $5,000; expenses increase by $5,000.
Assets decrease by $5,000; liabilities increase by $5,000.
Assets decrease by $5,000; owner equity decreases by $5,000.
Assets decrease by $5,000; revenues increase by $5,000.
questions.explanation: Cash out = assets down. Advertising is an expense → expenses reduce profit → profit reduces equity. So assets DOWN $5k, equity DOWN $5k. Equation stays balanced.

questions.q: What is a transaction?
choices: Two parties exchanging something of value
A type of commonly used accounting software
A category of merchandiser or retailer
An example of an online business document
questions.explanation: A transaction = any exchange of value between two parties. Buying, selling, borrowing, paying — all transactions.

questions.q: A company borrowed $80,000 cash from a bank. How does this transaction affect the accounting equation of the borrowing company?
choices: Assets increase by $80,000; liabilities increase by $80,000.
Assets increase by $80,000; owners' equity increases by $80,000.
Assets increase by $80,000; liabilities decrease by $80,000.
Assets increase by $80,000; revenues increase by $80,000.
questions.explanation: Cash comes in (asset UP) and you owe the bank (liability UP). Borrowing doesn't earn revenue — it creates debt. Equation: +$80k Assets = +$80k Liabilities + $0 Equity.

questions.q: What is the impact of expenses on the accounting equation?
choices: Expenses increase liabilities.
Expenses decrease owners' equity.
Expenses decrease liabilities.
Expenses increase owners' equity.
questions.explanation: Expenses reduce profit → profit flows to retained earnings → retained earnings is part of equity. So expenses DECREASE equity.

questions.q: Which type of account are accounts payable and notes payable both examples of?
choices: Liability
Asset
Expense
Equity
questions.explanation: 'Payable' = you OWE someone. All payables are liabilities. Accounts payable = owe suppliers. Notes payable = owe lenders.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the financial accounting cycle?
choices: To collect confidential information for management to use as a competitive tool
To gather information related to the expenses and income generated by a company
To turn information about transactions into financial statements
To produce and analyze a company's monthly bank statement
questions.explanation: The accounting cycle = the workflow that converts raw transactions into the big three financial statements. That's its whole job.

questions.q: According to the accounting equation, the amount of liabilities and equity must always be equal to another amount. What is that other amount?
choices: The sum of revenues and expenses
Assets
Cash
The sum of expenses and dividends
questions.explanation: The accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. So L + E = Assets. Always. Every balance sheet.

questions.q: Which item is an expense item?
choices: Loans payable
Cost of goods sold
Accounts receivable
Accounts payable
questions.explanation: COGS = expense (income statement). Payables = liabilities (balance sheet). Receivables = assets (balance sheet).

questions.q: How is gross profit computed?
choices: Sales minus cost of goods sold
Total assets minus total liabilities
Accounts receivable minus accounts payable
Total revenues minus total expenses
questions.explanation: Gross Profit = Sales − COGS. It's the first profit line on the income statement. Net income is Revenues − ALL expenses (the bottom line, different concept).

questions.q: Which type of account is retained earnings?
choices: Revenue
Liability
Equity
Asset
questions.explanation: Retained earnings = profits the company kept (didn't pay out as dividends). It's a component of EQUITY on the balance sheet.

questions.q: For purposes of cash flow classification in the statement of cash flows, which item is an operating activity?
choices: Buying equipment
Paying employees
Distributing dividends
Selling bonds
questions.explanation: CFS has 3 sections: Operating (day-to-day: paying employees, paying suppliers, receiving from customers), Investing (buying/selling long-term assets like equipment), Financing (stocks, bonds, dividends, loans).

questions.q: How does a classified balance sheet provide useful information to a decision maker?
choices: It distinguishes between current and long-term assets.
It distinguishes liabilities from expenses.
It provides data that are not publicly disclosed.
It provides data for a period of time instead of as a point in time.
questions.explanation: 'Classified' balance sheet means assets/liabilities are grouped into CURRENT (≤1 year) and LONG-TERM (>1 year). Helps users see liquidity at a glance.

questions.q: What information does a balance sheet provide to a decision maker?
choices: Summary of the operating performance of a company during a period
Summary of the cash flows of a company during a period
Summary of the operating performance of a company at a particular date
Summary of the financial position of a company at a particular date
questions.explanation: Balance sheet = SNAPSHOT at a single date (Dec 31, etc.). Shows financial position: what you own, owe, and equity. Income statement and cash flows cover a PERIOD.

questions.q: What is an account payable?
choices: The amount owed to a company that sold goods or services to a customer on credit
The amount to be paid by a company in repayment of both loans and dividends
The amount to be paid by a company for dividends to shareholders
The amount owed by a company that purchased goods or services from a supplier on credit
questions.explanation: Accounts PAYABLE = what YOU owe suppliers (credit purchases). Accounts RECEIVABLE = what customers owe YOU. Trap answer A is receivable.

questions.q: What is an example of a financial cost that would result from poor direct labor budgeting and planning?
choices: Delayed cash collections from credit customers
Increased depreciation costs for facilities
Increased hiring, training, and overtime costs
Excessive inventory storage costs
questions.explanation: Poor labor planning → emergency hiring, rushed training, paying overtime. Those are direct consequences of not forecasting workforce needs right.

questions.q: What does a manager have control over in a cost center?
choices: Revenues
Assets
Costs
Dividends
questions.explanation: 4 responsibility centers: Cost (costs only), Revenue (revenues only), Profit (both), Investment (profit + assets). The name tells you what's controlled.

questions.q: What should be considered when developing a measure to evaluate the performance of a manager?
choices: Only indirect costs
Only controllable costs
Only noncontrollable costs
Only centralized costs
questions.explanation: Cardinal rule of performance evaluation: only hold managers accountable for what they can CONTROL. Judging them on uncontrollable costs is unfair and demotivating.

questions.q: In some companies, the performance measures for profit center managers are heavily influenced by cost allocations downward from organizational units (such as company headquarters). Why is this a mistake?
choices: Revenues should not be included in the performance evaluation measure of a profit center manager.
Direct costs should not be included in the performance evaluation measure of a profit center manager.
Controllable costs should not be included in the performance evaluation measure of a profit center manager.
Uncontrollable costs should not be included in the performance evaluation measure of a profit center manager.
questions.explanation: HQ allocations (rent, exec salaries) are UNCONTROLLABLE by division managers. Including them in performance measures punishes managers for things they can't change.

questions.q: Which budget should include the expected cost of supplies used by the office staff of the corporate headquarters?
choices: Production budget
Sales budget
Administrative expense budget
Direct materials budget
questions.explanation: HQ office supplies = admin expense (period cost). Production/materials budgets are for manufacturing. Sales budget = revenue forecast.

questions.q: Which items are uncontrollable, external variables that make it difficult to forecast the level of sales?
choices: Direct labor and advertising expenditures
Selling price and sales effort
Customer tastes and economic conditions
Inventory level and product management
questions.explanation: Customer tastes and the economy are OUTSIDE the company's control. Pricing, advertising, labor, inventory are INTERNAL variables the company controls.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of budgets in a manufacturing business?
choices: Direct materials, sales, production
Sales, production, direct materials
Sales, direct materials, production
Production, direct materials, sales
questions.explanation: Master budget flow: SALES first (how much will we sell?) → PRODUCTION (how much do we make?) → DIRECT MATERIALS (what do we buy to make it?). Sales drives everything.

questions.q: Which type of business organization has a major focus on direct materials, direct labor, and overhead?
choices: Retail
Manufacturing
Service
Merchandising
questions.explanation: DM + DL + MOH = the 3 MANUFACTURING product costs. Retail/merchandising buy finished goods. Service has no physical product.

questions.q: What are the three primary functions that company managers use managerial accounting information for?
choices: Borrowing, repaying, and lending
Reporting, allowing, and negotiating
Operating, investing, and financing
Planning, controlling, and evaluating
questions.explanation: PCE: Planning (budgets), Controlling (vs actual), Evaluating (performance). Operating/investing/financing are CFS categories, different concept.

questions.q: What is the proper accounting for a product cost?
choices: Record as a financing cash flow
Record immediately as an expense
Record as an inventory cost until the item is sold
Record as a liability on the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Product costs (DM + DL + MOH) = capitalized as INVENTORY (asset) until the product is sold, then flow to COGS. Period costs expense immediately.

questions.q: How could a period cost be reported in an income statement?
choices: As cost of goods manufactured
As cost of goods sold
As an administrative expense
As manufacturing overhead
questions.explanation: Period costs = Selling + Administrative. They show up as S&A expenses on the income statement, never touched inventory. COGS and COGM are product cost concepts.

questions.q: A retail company purchased inventory costing $100,000. By the end of the year, inventory costing $75,000 had been sold. How is the remaining $25,000 in inventory reported in the financial statements?
choices: As an asset in the balance sheet
As manufacturing overhead in the income statement
As an administrative expense in the income statement
As a liability in the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Unsold inventory = ASSET on balance sheet (current asset). Only the $75k sold becomes COGS. This is why product costs are inventoriable — they sit as an asset until sold.

questions.q: How are the wages of cashiers classified in a merchandising company?
choices: Cost of goods sold
Manufacturing overhead
Work-in-process inventory
Selling expense
questions.explanation: Cashiers = point-of-sale staff = SELLING expense (period cost). Merchandising has no manufacturing, no WIP. COGS is the cost of goods, not the people who sell them.

questions.q: How are wages of office staff in a company headquarters building classified?
choices: Direct labor
Indirect labor
Manufacturing overhead
Administrative expense
questions.explanation: HQ office staff = ADMIN expense (period cost, not tied to production). Direct/indirect labor and MOH are all manufacturing concepts — HQ is not in the factory.

questions.q: Which label is given to the cost of the wood used in the construction of a piece of wooden furniture?
choices: Direct labor
Manufacturing overhead
Selling and administrative
Direct materials
questions.explanation: Wood = primary input physically in the furniture = DIRECT MATERIALS. If it can be traced directly to the product in measurable amounts, it's DM.

questions.q: Which label is given to the cost of electricity in a furniture factory?
choices: Direct labor
Manufacturing overhead
Administrative expenses
Direct materials
questions.explanation: Factory electricity = supports production but not traceable to a specific product = MANUFACTURING OVERHEAD (indirect). If it were HQ electricity, it'd be admin expense.

questions.q: What is the sequence of the flow of costs through a manufacturing operation?
choices: Raw materials, work-in-process, finished goods, cost of goods sold
Finished goods, cost of goods sold, raw materials, work-in-process
Cost of goods sold, raw materials, work-in-process, finished goods
Work-in-process, raw materials, finished goods, cost of goods sold
questions.explanation: Flow: RM → WIP → FG → COGS. Buy materials, start making them (WIP), finish them (FG), sell them (COGS). MEMORIZE THIS ORDER.

questions.q: What is the CVP equation?
choices: Sales - fixed costs - administrative costs = profit
Sales - cost of goods sold - fixed costs = profit
Sales - variable costs - overhead costs = profit
Sales - variable costs - fixed costs = profit
questions.explanation: CVP (Cost-Volume-Profit): Sales − Variable Costs − Fixed Costs = Profit. The core managerial accounting equation. Everything else derives from this.

questions.q: Which cost category is not formally tracked in a company's accounting system?
choices: Direct costs
Indirect costs
Out-of-pocket costs
Opportunity costs
questions.explanation: Opportunity costs = value of the road NOT taken. Real but never recorded. Direct, indirect, and out-of-pocket are all actually spent dollars that hit the books.

questions.q: A company reports: Total sales revenue = $250,000. Number of units sold = 50,000 units. Variable costs = $100,000. If the company is operating at its break-even point, what is the company's total contribution margin?
questions.explanation: CM = Sales − Variable Costs = $250,000 − $100,000 = $150,000. At break-even, CM EQUALS Fixed Costs (so Fixed Costs also = $150k). CM itself is just Sales − VC.

questions.q: A company reports: Price per unit = $25. Variable costs per unit = $15. Fixed costs = $15,000. Given these data, what is the variable cost ratio?
questions.explanation: VC Ratio = Variable Cost per unit ÷ Price per unit = $15 ÷ $25 = 60%. CM Ratio would be the other 40%. Fixed costs are irrelevant to this ratio.

questions.q: Why is the concept of relevant range important to a manager?
choices: Inside the relevant range, the total fixed cost can change.
Inside the relevant range, the variable cost per unit can increase.
Outside the relevant range, the variable cost per unit can change.
Outside the relevant range, the variable cost per unit stays constant.
questions.explanation: Relevant range = the activity level where cost behavior assumptions HOLD. INSIDE: fixed costs stay fixed, variable costs per unit stay constant. OUTSIDE: all bets off (bulk discounts, new machinery needed, etc.).

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes applied manufacturing overhead?
choices: The total manufacturing costs other than direct materials
The amount of manufacturing overhead that is assigned to each employee
The total manufacturing costs other than direct labor
The amount of manufacturing overhead that is assigned to the goods produced
questions.explanation: APPLIED overhead = the MOH charged to products using the predetermined rate. It's what lands on the goods produced, not on employees or totals.

questions.q: What is the label given to the quantity computed as estimated overhead costs divided by estimated level of activity?
choices: Underapplied overhead rate
Predetermined overhead rate
Forecasted overhead rate
Indirect overhead rate
questions.explanation: Predetermined Overhead Rate = Estimated MOH ÷ Estimated Activity (like machine hours or labor hours). Set at start of year, used to apply MOH. Under/over-applied happens when actual differs from applied.

questions.q: In a job order costing system, what is the proper accounting for a product cost?
choices: It is reported as a part of general expenses.
It is reported as a part of administrative expenses.
It is reported as a part of cost of goods sold.
It is reported as an expense when it occurs.
questions.explanation: Product costs in any system (job order, process, ABC) flow through inventory → COGS when sold. They are NEVER expensed immediately and NEVER part of general/admin expenses.

questions.q: Which item is a period cost?
choices: Wages for factory quality control inspectors
Rent on factory robotic equipment in an airplane manufacturer
Wages of maintenance workers in the factory building
Utility bills to heat the headquarters building
questions.explanation: HQ utilities = period cost (admin). Anything with 'factory' in the description = product cost (MOH). QC inspectors, factory equipment rent, factory maintenance are all MOH.

questions.q: Which statement is true with respect to activity-based costing (ABC) systems?
choices: Implementing an ABC system requires only a careful calculation of total direct labor hours.
Implementing an ABC system requires very little analysis of the factors that create overhead costs.
An ABC system allocates overhead based on multiple activities.
An ABC system completely eliminates all overhead costs.
questions.explanation: ABC uses MULTIPLE cost drivers (setups, inspections, machine hours, etc.) instead of one blunt rate. It requires DETAILED analysis. It doesn't eliminate overhead — it allocates it more accurately.

questions.q: How is overhead allocated in an ABC system?
choices: Cost pool multiplied by number of cost driver events
Activity rate multiplied by number of cost driver events
Budgeted overhead multiplied by expected number of direct labor hours
Sum of materials and labor cost multiplied by number of units
questions.explanation: ABC formula: Activity Rate × # of Cost Driver Events. Activity Rate = cost pool ÷ total driver events. Then applied per product/job by multiplying times the events consumed.

questions.q: In an ABC system, which name is given to a numerical measure reflecting the amount of a cost associated with a particular overhead cost activity?
choices: Cost system
Cost driver
Cost metric
Cost pool
questions.explanation: Cost POOL = the dollar amount grouped by activity (e.g., 'setup costs = $50,000'). Cost DRIVER = what causes it (e.g., 'number of setups'). Don't swap them.

questions.q: How are production costs treated in a process costing system?
choices: Costs are accumulated by process and averaged over all products made during the period.
Costs are assigned to a selling, general, and administrative expense account during the period.
Costs are assigned to the actual manufacturing overhead account during the period.
Costs are assigned to specific jobs or products made during the period.
questions.explanation: Process costing = mass production (cereal, gasoline). Accumulate costs by PROCESS (mixing, bottling), average over all units. Job order assigns to specific jobs.

questions.q: How is the production cost per unit computed in a process costing system?
choices: Amount of direct labor cost divided by the number of direct labor hours used during a particular period of time
Amount of overhead cost divided by the number of units completed during a particular period of time
Amount of direct materials cost divided by the quantity of direct materials used during a particular period of time
Amount of total production cost divided by the number of units completed during a particular period of time
questions.explanation: Process cost per unit = TOTAL PRODUCTION COSTS ÷ UNITS COMPLETED. Simple average across all identical units. The other options use partial numerators — wrong.

questions.q: For which production process is process costing the appropriate costing method to use?
choices: Constructing a high-rise office building
Building custom-made furniture
Producing made-to-order industrial equipment
Refining gasoline in a petroleum facility
questions.explanation: Gasoline refining = continuous, identical output = PROCESS costing. Construction/custom/made-to-order = unique each time = JOB ORDER costing.

questions.q: Which overhead allocation method should be used for a business that mass-produces breakfast cereal?
choices: ABC costing
Job order costing
Product-line costing
Process costing
questions.explanation: Mass production of identical units = PROCESS costing. Cereal, chemicals, gasoline, paint — all process. ABC is for complex multi-product overhead allocation.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence for the flow of costs through a job order costing system?
choices: Raw materials inventory, work-in-process inventory, cost of goods sold, finished goods inventory
Raw materials inventory, finished goods inventory, cost of goods sold, work-in-process inventory
Raw materials inventory, work-in-process inventory, finished goods inventory, cost of goods sold
Raw materials inventory, cost of goods sold, work-in-process inventory, finished goods inventory
questions.explanation: RM → WIP → FG → COGS. Same in both job order and process. Buy materials → make them (WIP) → finish (FG) → sell (COGS). Memorize this path.

questions.q: Which type of company cannot use job order costing?
choices: Road construction
Tax accountant for wealthy people
Petroleum refining plant
Building construction
questions.explanation: Petroleum refining = continuous identical output = MUST use process costing. Construction and custom tax work = unique jobs = job order fits perfectly.

questions.q: What is an example of direct materials?
choices: Cost of sandpaper in making wood furniture
Cost of robotic equipment in making automobiles
Cost of aluminum in making an airplane
Cost of saws and hammers in constructing a house
questions.explanation: Direct materials = physically IN the product, traceable in measurable amounts. Aluminum in a plane = DM. Sandpaper, robots, tools = MOH (indirect — they help produce but aren't IN the product).

questions.q: What is an example of direct labor?
choices: Wages for furniture assemblers in a wood furniture manufacturer
Wages for factory quality control inspectors
Wages for marketing staff in company headquarters
Wages for accounting staff in company headquarters
questions.explanation: Direct labor = workers who TOUCH the product. Assemblers build the furniture = DL. QC inspectors = indirect (MOH). Marketing and accounting = period costs (S&A).

questions.q: What is an example of manufacturing overhead?
choices: Cost of aluminum in making an airplane
Cost of sandpaper in making wood furniture
Cost of concrete in making a road
Cost of bricks in making a building
questions.explanation: Sandpaper = INDIRECT material (not physically IN final furniture in meaningful amount) = MOH. Aluminum, concrete, bricks are all primary physical inputs = DIRECT MATERIALS.

questions.q: What is horizontal analysis in the context of financial statement analysis?
choices: Calculating each line item as a percentage of total sales for the same year
Calculating the percentage change in each line item from one year to the next
Comparing one company's financial statements to a competitor's financial statements
Analyzing the relationship between current and long-term liabilities
questions.explanation: HORIZONTAL analysis = trends OVER TIME (year-to-year % change). VERTICAL analysis = each item as % of base (usually total sales) in the SAME year. Horizontal scans left-to-right across years.

questions.q: Based on an analysis showing operating expenses rising sharply over two years while sales grew more slowly, what should management be concerned about?
choices: The increase in interest expenses over the past two years
The increase in income taxes over the past two years
The increase in operating expenses over the past two years
The increase in production cost over the past two years
questions.explanation: If operating expenses are outpacing sales growth, operating margin is squeezed. This is the profitability threat management must address. Interest/taxes are not operating, and production is a subset, not the whole story.

questions.q: Which action would make the profitability of the company in 20X9 the same as in 20X7?
choices: Decreasing the proportion of operating income to sales by about 2%
Increasing the proportion of gross profit to sales by about 2%
Increasing the operating expenses by about $20,000
Paying back interest expenses earlier in the year
questions.explanation: To restore earlier profitability: improve gross profit margin. Gross profit % has to RISE, not fall, and operating expenses must fall, not rise. B is the only action that directly increases profitability.

questions.q: In the Whole Pine cash flow analysis, how should a column chart showing cash availability for each month be titled?
choices: Cash Analysis
Monthly Receipts
Total Cash Available
Whole Pine Cash
questions.explanation: Task 60.1 in the workbook specifies the exact title: 'Total Cash Available'. MyEducator grades titles EXACTLY. Don't improvise on chart titles.

questions.q: Why is the net cash for December negative while total sales for December are the highest out of the months from October through December?
choices: December general and administrative expenses are expected to be much higher.
Credit sales are disproportionately low with respect to total sales compared to other months.
Total cash available does not reflect December sales because there was a high volume of credit sales.
December cash use is disproportionally high with respect to total sales compared to other months.
questions.explanation: December has $50k equipment purchase + $55k cash dividend on top of normal outflows, pushing Total Cash Outflows to $454k. Sales are high but cash USE is disproportionately higher. The giant outflows, not receipt timing, drive the negative.

questions.q: How can Whole Pine avoid having negative net cash flows in December?
choices: Promote cash sales with the goal of having $230,000 in cash sales and only $210,000 in credit sales.
Postpone purchasing the new equipment and do not pay cash dividends to shareholders.
Collect 50% of the credit sales in the month of credit sales and 30% in the month following the credit sales.
Instead of paying for credit purchases of inventory a month after the purchase, pay two months after the purchase.
questions.explanation: The $50k equipment + $55k dividend = $105k of DISCRETIONARY December outflows. Postponing both eliminates the cash shortfall directly. The other options tinker with collection timing or payment timing, which help less and risk supplier/customer relationships.
